utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we ready for the witness, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor. If I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to deal now, please, with the following dates, the 18th, 19th, 20th and 21st. May we deal, please, with the evening of the 18th of November. Now, you've already told us that on the 18th you had sent various faxes. Can you in very general terms tell us what the general atmosphere was on the 18th and what occurred, please, and can you try and keep your answers short?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The atmosphere was very difficult, because previous information that we received that on the 18th the evacuation would start turned out not to materialise. An increasing number of civilians was arriving at the hospital and since we had ran out of food and water and blankets and since there were many women, children and the elderly, the situation was very grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many civilians actually came to the hospital on the 18th, in very general terms?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say, but more than 500. The entire upper storey which previously was vacant was filled with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did those civilians remain at the hospital that day and afterwards? Can you tell us what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, and the following days, rather up until the following day they remained at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Where were they kept? Where were they staying?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the main hospital building, where we stayed in the underground premises, rather, the basement, and they were in the hallway on the ground floor and the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you either see or were you aware of any evacuation of civilians on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the negotiations that were conducted in Zagreb, it was said that civilians would be evacuated as well. Marin Vidic was in charge of the evacuation of civilians. He was the government commissioner for the municipality of Vukovar. On the 18th the -- there should have been an evacuation of the wounded in the hospital whereas on the 19th and the 20th the civilians were supposed to be evacuated. This is what I learned on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move to the 19th, please? What was your expectation? What did you think was going to happen on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my previous conversation with Minister Hebrang on Monday, the 18th, instead of arriving on Monday, the 18th, the Red Cross was supposed to arrive at 8.00 on the 19th, arrive at the hospital. Therefore, we expected that the evacuation would take one day longer, since the European monitors had called to say that they weren't able to arrive on that day, so they were expected on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say 8.00, is that 8.00 in the morning or 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So who actually arrived on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 8.00 in the morning, on the 19th, nobody arrived. I called Minister Hebrang again and was told that he was on his way to Vinkovci and Nustar to await a convoy there. I spoke to Dr. Branic. I spoke twice to General Raseta and informed him that nobody had come, that there was no International Red Cross there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did General Raseta then say to you when you informed him of this fact?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on his information, the International Red Cross was in Vukovar, and was by the bridge. I understood this to mean the railway bridge. Therefore, Marin Vidic, another associate of mine, Senka Vuko, and I went to the railway bridge which was located near the hospital to see whether the representatives of the ICRC were there. That was the first time that we saw trucks full of soldiers there, full of soldiers and reservists, who were there at the bridge and were directing civilians who were in a street called Priljevo into the trucks. That was on the 19th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. You've told us, I think that you spoke to General Raseta more than once. You've told us about one telephone conversation. What about the other telephone conversations? Did you phone him that day again?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called again to say that they were not on the bridge. The soldiers who were at the bridge told me that they knew nothing about any Red Cross whatsoever, and that they were told to go up until the bridge but not cross the bridge, to go to the hospital. I called General Raseta once again and he tried to calm me down, telling me that everything would be all right, and that I should try to get in touch with Colonel Mrksic because he was in charge of that area. I told him that I didn't know how I could get in touch with him and he told me I needn't worry, that they would find me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So did you speak to Colonel Mrksic that day as --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was, please and how it arose?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 19th, on Tuesday. I received a call. I know that Colonel Mrksic told me that everything would be all right, that he was from Vukovar himself, that we attended the same high school, and that everything would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you actually meet Colonel Mrksic that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I met with him on Tuesday, on the 19th, in the afternoon, in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us how that arose that you went to Negoslavci, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 12.00, a jeep arrived at the hospital, carrying an officer of the JNA and some soldiers. I went outside and inquired whether the International Red Cross and the European monitors were accompanying them. They said no. He said that he hadn't seen them anywhere in the vicinity. I told him that I was expecting them to arrive at the hospital and asked where I could find them, and then he told me that he had seen some vehicles of European monitors in the village of Negoslavci. Then I asked him whether he could take me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you go there with him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told my colleagues at the hospital and Marin Vidic that I was going to Negoslavci. Then this officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, I don't know his name or rank, drove me to the village of Negoslavci, to a private house there that had -- that was designated as the Main Staff. It had a sign saying something to that effect. I went inside and I met Colonel Mrksic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were expecting monitors or the Red Cross. They weren't there. Did you mention this to Colonel Mrksic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did he say about the absence of monitors and the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the monitors would arrive and the Red Cross as well, but that that was not important, but because they were just in the way. They were preventing us from agreeing on evacuation among ourselves. It was easier for us to do that than getting the international observers and the Red Cross involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When that suggestion was made to you, how did you react to that? What was your view?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that we could not negotiate on evacuation because the agreement had already been signed between the Croatian government and the representative of the JNA, General Raseta, International Red Cross, and European monitors. I said that it had already been agreed that the hospital ought to have been evacuated. That was supposed to happen on the previous day. That the routes had already been agreed upon and that people were awaiting us in Nustar. I told him that the situation at the hospital was very difficult, that there was gaseous gangrene spreading around, and that evacuation should begin as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you discuss to him -- did you discuss with him the requirement or your desire to have the monitors actually there when the evacuation was going to occur?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that included the agreement signed in Zagreb, namely that the evacuation would be organised by the International Red Cross in the presence of European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you had been informed that monitors were in Negoslavci and you went to Negoslavci originally to see them. Did you actually see them when you were there visiting Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- as I was leaving the meeting, as I left the house, at the end of that road, I saw a white vehicle, and I asked the person escorting me to take me there so that I could speak to European monitors. He said that he had to get an approval for that, and after he asked somebody, I assume that he had asked General -- Colonel Mrksic because this is where he took me, he came back saying that that wasn't necessary, that he would take me back to the hospital, and that the monitors would arrive as soon as possible at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You say that he had asked permission from someone, you assumed it was Colonel Mrksic. What led to that assumption? Was there anything that he did or said?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came back from the vehicle, went into the building and then came back again. I thought that he had probably gone back to ask the colonel but I don't know. I remained in the vehicle waiting for him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, were you able to speak to the monitors, as they appeared to be?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he said that he had to take me back to the hospital. Later, while I was at the hospital, none of the monitors showed up. The first time I talked to the monitors was when I was in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At what time approximately did you arrive back at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the situation like at the hospital when you returned?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon return, we came across a lot of people walking in the streets in columns. Among them I recognised my mother. I asked the officer who drove me to stop. I said that that was my mother there. So my mother came into the car and she said that they were taking them to Velepromet. I asked her where my parents in law were and she said that they had been taken out earlier and then once we arrived at the hospital, I saw a lot of soldiers around the hospital and reservists, among whom I recognised one of our former employees, who worked at the hospital before the war. I asked the man who drove me to get my parents in law from Velepromet and bring them to the hospital so that we could stay all together there. And then he recognised -- then he suggested that Bogdan Kuzmic, the man I recognised among the reservists, should go and get them. However, he did not do that within the following hour, and then I repeated my request, wrote down the names of my father- and mother-in-law on a piece of paper, and then one of the people escorting me brought them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you refer to soldiers, what soldiers are we talking about? Are we talking about Croatian soldiers, JNA, TO? Are you able to distinguish or can you tell the Court exactly what those soldiers were doing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army. The reservists and some volunteers who wore various kinds of uniform, then the military police of the Yugoslav army, which supposedly secured the entrance into the hospital. That was according to the officer who accompanied me. However, when I returned in the afternoon, I saw the soldiers and reservists going through the hospital. The hospital was overflowing with people, the wounded, patients, civilians, who had arrived in the previous two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you use the phrase "soldiers were going through the hospital," what sort of things were they doing when they were going through the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. To tell you the truth, I don't know who was milling through the hospital. I know that I heard that Bogdan Kuzmic who used to work there and who was now in the capacity of a reservist was going through the hospital appearing to look for people and asking for names. People were afraid because it seemed that he was on the side of those who were killing us. I saw Jovic, Sasa, talking to some soldiers. I asked him to come to my office and then I told him that he should remain in the room where he had been previously, awaiting the International Red Cross together with us, and he said that he would do that. Then I was told that some volunteers wanted to enter the hospital. I came out and I saw some people wearing camouflage uniforms and helmets with some white ribbons, with cockades on their helmets entering the hospital alongside the Yugoslav People's Army soldiers who were supposedly guarding the entrance. I told them that they were not allowed inside the hospital. They were aggressive. They were angry with me. Dr. Ivankovic came out from the surgical clinic and he told them that they should stop with it, that they should calm down, and then he said to me, "Vesna, you should not say anything else. Just go back to your room and sit there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that names were being asked for. Was there anything else that was occurring apart from names that caused you concern at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was afraid. Mrs. Zeljka Zgonjanin came to tell me that on the floor above us, they were starting to separate the men from women and children. I went out to see what was going on and I could see through the main door that they were taking men outside and putting them on the trucks and driving them away. That was the first time I met Major Sljivancanin. I asked him why they were separating the men, and where they were taking them when we were actually all awaiting evacuation and expecting the first evacuation of the wounded. He was quite arrogant and he told me that I should not meddle in the affairs which were no concern of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with this piece of evidence in perhaps a little more detail. You say that you saw men being taken outside and placed in trucks. Who was actually taking the men outside?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers were, and putting them on lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the men were being taken from where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the main building of the hospital, where they had assembled from all the surrounding shelters all over the town, alongside with women and children, to await evacuation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you use the word "men" it can mean many things. It can mean armed soldiers, it can mean doctors in white coats. It can mean any sort of description. Was there anything that made you --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that I was able to see, all of them were civilians wearing civilian clothes. Men from the ground floor and first floor were leaving the building and getting on to those lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you express any direct concern to Sljivancanin himself about these men being taken away with no monitors being present?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did, as I've said before. That's why I came outside to request protection. I asked where they were taking them but he was quite arrogant. He said I had no business being there asking these things and I should go back to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but the question is really quite specific. Did you actually mention to him that there was an agreement, an evacuation agreement, where monitors were supposed to be present?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I told him that we were expecting the International Red Cross and European monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And his reply about the European monitors coming was what?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said they would be there eventually, that I should just go back to my office and wait there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What time was that about, when you spoke to Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 5.00 or 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many trucks did you see come or how many civilian, male civilians, did you see taken away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only outside for a brief while. I saw the truck outside the entrance and I saw people getting on to it but I can't tell you exactly how many trucks there were or how many people for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was the first time that you met Major Sljivancanin. Did you meet him again that day or evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him again that evening. He entered my office and said, "You have been waiting for the Red Cross for so long. Well, they are here now." He was accompanied by two Red Cross representatives, one of them I recognised later, Nicholas Borsinger. There was another rather small man who introduced himself as a doctor, and there was an interpreter present too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak to Nicholas Borsinger about what had occurred prior to his arrival?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At last someone was there, more specifically the International Red Cross. I had been convinced that they would be the ones conducting our evacuation in much the same way as the previous evacuation had been organised by the Medecins Sans Frontieres one month before. I told them that we had spent two days waiting for them and that the situation in the hospital was very difficult. I told them we were quite disappointed to see them arrive this late. He said that they brought with them some help, some medical equipment and medicine, that perhaps we could use this to alleviate the situation. I told them that it was already too late, that perhaps this might prove useful but that the main thing was for an evacuation to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about the wounded? How were you going to deal with the wounded with Nicholas Borsinger? How was he to ascertain who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a leading question. The witness said exactly what she had done. She talked to Borsinger and now the Prosecutor is suggesting that they were talking about the wounded. I think this is putting a subject to the witness. She was quite clear about what their conversation had been about. The first question by the Prosecutor should have been, Did you in fact talk about anything else, and then a question like this might have followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In my submission I'm perfectly entitled to ask a witness whether there were any specific topics mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You certainly are, Mr. Moore. The correct position lies between your position and that of Mr. Lukic, and we won't waste time negotiating it. You may certainly turn the witness's attention to a new topic, but there seems to be concern about this conversation and this area so you should not lead and you should not get into the position of suggesting what may have been the conversation, and your questions went too far in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember any other topic that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about the difficult situation in the hospital. I was adamant that we should go to the hospital so that he could see for himself what the situation was, or, rather, how desperate. I must say I was disappointed. My impression was that Mr. Borsinger was scared of all that he could see around him of the situation that he ended up in. I was quite disappointed. This was different from what we had all expected from the International Red Cross and the international community as a whole. Major Sljivancanin, who was with him, asked if we had made any evacuation lists. I said that we had drawn up lists of people who were wounded with their specific diagnoses. I gave him one bundle of those lists. He was adamant that I should hand over all the lists that I had or rather all the copies. I asked, "Why? Aren't we supposed to keep some of the copies?" But he insisted that he should have all of the copies in order to be able to compare. I yielded and gave him all the copies. He asked me if these were all the people to be evacuated and I told him these were all the wounded people in the hospital but that there were names that weren't included on the list, such as nurses and doctors, family members of those wounded, and hospital staff. At this point I expected that the International Red Cross people would remain with us throughout the evacuation. I expected that the wounded would be categorised, classified, according to the seriousness of their injuries and according to when they should be evacuated and where to. Mr. Borsinger then told me that they were unable to stay, that they were supposed to drive back to Belgrade. He said they would return the following morning at 8.00. I was shocked by this. I couldn't believe my ears. I said, "Why? Why don't you stay with us until the evacuation is completed?" He said that there was still nothing he could do about this evacuation. This was an additional surprise and shock. I was expecting the International Red Cross to organise the evacuation itself pursuant to the agreement that had been signed, but he said he had no power over this, that he had no power whatsoever over how exactly the JNA would be organising this evacuation. I asked him to stay with us to witness the evacuation, even if he was himself in no position to actually organise one. He said he would be back the next morning at 8.00 and off they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When Mr. Borsinger informed you that he would be returning the next day, namely the 20th, at 8.00 in the morning, did he say that in the presence of Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in my office, all of them, Major Sljivancanin and he. There was this doctor who said that he was from Switzerland. He stayed for a brief while and then left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Presumably, then, Mr. Nicholas Borsinger left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about giving lists to Major Sljivancanin. Did you actually give Borsinger a list as well?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave first copy to Borsinger and the remaining copies to Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who were on that list, can we just in general terms try and assess how many people were on the list that you gave?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list contained about 400 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the 400 people, were they subdivided in any way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those seriously injured, who required an ambulance to be transported, there were about 180 of those. The remaining patients were able to move or half mobile, as it were, and could leave on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that Borsinger and Sljivancanin and the others all left. Did you remain in the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not that night. Later on, Sljivancanin returned on his own and asked me to track down Dr. Antic. He wanted to speak to her. She left to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That clearly relates to in the hospital, but did you leave the hospital was the question? Or the question actually was, did you remain in the hospital that night?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was saying. I was picked up by an officer, a captain, who was there with Sljivancanin. He took me away. He said he had been told to take me back to Negoslavci, which is what he did, and that's where I spent the night, between the 19th and the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with Negoslavci? When you were going there, who did you think you were going to see? Or the reason that you were going there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my way there, the thought occurred to me that I might meet Colonel Mrksic there because I had met him before in the same building. However, when I arrived, I didn't see Colonel Mrksic. Major Sljivancanin was there and another man was standing next to him. I think this other man was a captain because that's how they referred to him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal, please, with this meeting with Sljivancanin and the gentleman whom you believed was a captain. Where did you actually meet Sljivancanin and the captain?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Negoslavci, the same building where I had previously met Colonel Mrksic on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, was it in a different office, a different part? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same office, the same room, as far as I know, where I had previously met Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was Sljivancanin standing or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both seated at a table. I sat down opposite Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have a discussion with Sljivancanin at this table?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or, rather, he started questioning me. He questioned me about the whereabouts of the Croatian soldiers, about the whereabouts of Jastreb. Jastreb was the nickname of Vukovar's defence commander. I told him I didn't know. The last time I had been with him was days before. He was quite gruff and quite strict. He said how was it possible I had no idea who had been killing his lads and his soldiers? I said I simply didn't know who had been killing them and likewise I had no idea why he, Sljivancanin, had brought them there in the first place, in order to destroy Vukovar. The other man seated next to him said I should watch my mouth because they had other methods to -- they knew for a fact that I had to know all these things because they had been listening in to all my conversations, phone conversations, with Zagreb. I said I had no idea what they wanted me to tell them, that there was no way I could help them about Jastreb's or the soldiers' whereabouts. I said that we, the hospital staff, had been treating everyone alike, Croatian soldiers, JNA soldiers, Serb soldiers, civilians. Sljivancanin then started taunting me, asking me how much I believed Tudjman was prepared to pay in order to have me released, whether I would be my same humanitarian self in one of their other hospitals at Petrova Gora. I felt miserable and I was no longer willing to engage in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did that conversation last?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say but I think about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you remain at Negoslavci that evening or were you taken back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called one of the soldiers and told him to take me somewhere to spend the night. I requested that I be driven back to the hospital. He said there was no way he could allow that because there, there were shoot-outs so they sent me to a building which they were using as some sort of war hospital. In passing, I saw some mattresses on which soldiers were lying. They took me through a long hall which was used as a dormitory, to another smaller one where I sat down on a bed and spent the night there. At 6.00 sharp the following morning, another soldier came along to take me away. He drove me in a jeep and Marin Vidic was already in the vehicle when I got in. So he drove both of us back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal, please, with when you return to the hospital on the morning? You said that at 6.00 sharp you left Negoslavci. How long did it take you to get back to the Vukovar Hospital, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you got back to the hospital, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my office, which we referred to at the time as the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were in your office, did you remain in your office?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in my office. I was guarded by a soldier who was carrying a rifle. Sljivancanin said that I should convene a staff meeting of the hospital at 7.00 sharp in a large conference room big enough to hold all of the hospital's personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, just before we go on to that, you said that you were detained by a soldier in your office. Did he say anything to you at that time while you were in your office sitting with him? Did he explain why he was there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he had been told to be in the room. The phones kept ringing but he would not allow me to pick up the phone. At first he answered the calls but then after some time he stopped answering the calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you speak to him about answering the telephone or using the telephone?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I inquired why he was refusing to allow me to answer the phone. There had been calls from Zagreb from the health ministry, from the government, from all over. I asked him to allow me to answer the phone, to convey the situation to whoever was on the other end, and he said that he had been given orders to prevent me from answering the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we move on, please, Major Sljivancanin? You have told us that he came and told you to convene a meeting at 7.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that we should assemble all of our medical staff in a large room that was big enough to hold a meeting with everybody there. I asked nurse Biba and my other associates to inform all the doctors and all the chief nurses to come for a meeting to this room where plaster casts can be made in peace time, that being the largest room in the entire hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is a meeting at 7.00. You've already told us that the previous evening there had been a discussion in the presence of Sljivancanin where the evacuation was to be at 8.00. Did you mention to Sljivancanin that the monitors would be coming that day or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean? When did I mention that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm asking if you did.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, you mean? On Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The 20th. You've told us you got back on the 20th. You've told us that you were in the morning --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just bade my time. I was hoping that as Borsinger had announced, they would be there at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In relation to the actual meeting itself, how long did it take to gather all the parties?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think between 15 and 20 minutes, then everyone was there. The room was nearly full. In addition to Sljivancanin, there were doctors there wearing JNA uniforms, about five or six of them, I think. Sljivancanin gave a speech, explaining to everyone that the JNA had just successfully liberated Vukovar and that all the hospitals would now be within the jurisdiction of the military hospital in Belgrade. He said that all the personnel should be classified according to whether they wanted to leave and be evacuated or stay and work at the hospital. He said that I was no longer in charge, that I was no longer manager, but that the military medical academy was now taking over the hospital. That soldier then walked me back to my office. I waited for the International Red Cross to come. As I was waiting, my mother entered my room to see if I was there, if everything was okay. She told me that my father-in-law had left the hospital. I asked where did he go? And she said that a soldier had passed by saying that all those who were able to walk should leave. He grabbed the opportunity because he had great pains in his leg and he had trouble just sitting where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to deal with the meeting itself. You've told us that all the medical staff were there. Did you see -- perhaps you could be kind enough to -- when you were at the meeting, did you see any exchange between JNA doctors and some of what I will call the Vukovar doctor hospitals -- hospital doctors?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that some people recognised each other. One of my colleagues recognised some of the doctors, and he went to greet him but the other wouldn't talk to him. I personally didn't recognise any of the doctors. I didn't know who they were. Later on, I heard that one of them went by the last name of Ivezic. I also heard some other names but I didn't know these people before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, did any of the doctors who worked in the hospital have children, sons or daughters, who had visited Vukovar or had come to Vukovar on the 18th, 19th, as part of the JNA contingent?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the son of Dr. Ivankovic came to the hospital with the volunteers who were calling themselves White Eagles. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what about Dr. Ivankovic? Did he stay or leave?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He immediately declared that he would stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about the way the Vukovar Hospital had been used throughout the struggle prior to the surrender of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean there at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There at the meeting or just after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I have no information to that effect. Later on, I gave a statement in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica about that, as well as in the barracks in Vukovar, but in the hospital itself, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain at the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact amount of time, but perhaps after an hour, this same officer who had taken me to Negoslavci came, saying that he had orders to take Marin Vidic and me to the meeting with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did they say there was going to be the meeting with the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say anything. He simply said he would take us to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you mention anything to him about that the International Red Cross were coming at 8.00 that morning and it would not be necessary?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that he was issued orders to take us to the meeting with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when -- where were you taken, then, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Sajmiste. We went to a room where there was a young man in the military police uniform who told us we should just sit there and that woe come and fetch us in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did anybody come to collect you from that room at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody came until the evening hours. A soldier came, bringing in a sausage and some bread. That was at around three in the afternoon. Then once again, the same person who had brought us there walked into the room in the evening, saying that there had been some changes, that the evacuation had been carried out, and that we had to stay -- spend the night in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you'd been told you were going to a meeting with the Red Cross apparently that morning, clearly didn't do so, and then were told that there was a change, did you say anything to that officer about those changes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything to the officer because he was simply issued orders to drive us there. I expected that somebody in charge would come, such as Sljivancanin or Mrksic. However, none of them came. They came to fetch me at 10 in the evening. Marin had to stay on there. They didn't take him out. They only took me to give the statement in the barracks in a room where there were a number of officers, a woman wearing a uniform. There were cameramen. They recorded this. They asked me to give a statement about the functioning of the hospital and my own role during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, just before you proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know when the Court is considering taking a break. I'll explain why so there is no problem about it. I can proceed quite easily. If one looks at the hard copy that the Court has, one can see on the index number 6. The doctor does not know to what I am referring at this time but the Defence do. This is a document that was created by Dr. Bosanac last week when I went to Vukovar. It has not been -- it has been shown to the Defence, as soon it was possible to do so, but has not been admitted in as an exhibit in a formal way. I felt it was only fair that the Defence should see this prior to Dr. Bosanac giving evidence. I was actually going to deal with it but I wanted to see if there were any objections to that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we understand that you suggest an adjournment now so that you can have discussions with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the Defence know that I clearly was intending to use it at some time. We had referred to perhaps Dr. Bosanac coming back on another occasion to deal with other matters. I can deal with it now or I can deal with it later. I'm quite relaxed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It could be yes or it could be no. I don't really mind one way or the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. Is the answer that you were planning to discuss with the Defence during the break what course should be taken about this matter at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm wondering if the Defence want to make any objection now because if they do, I'm quite happy to argue it now. It's not something that they have been caught unawares, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic, you're volunteering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness entered the courtroom, we were informed by the Prosecutor that he had been in Vukovar, or rather that he had talked to Mrs. Bosanac and that she had given him some documents which had not previously been disclosed to us and that he would perhaps put a question based on those documents. At the time he didn't told us that this would involve this document marked as annex 6 in this set of documents. He simply said that this involved some documentation from the hospital. This is what we discussed. We said that in principle, the position of the Defence would be such that they do not want to cross-examine a witness before familiarising themselves in detail with a document and obtain instructions from their clients. This is the first time that my colleagues and I hear that it pertains to this particular document. I don't know what this entails. As far as I can see, this is a list of victims and I don't know if this pertains to this document, that this is what he talked about with Mrs. Bosanac. If that was the case we would ask the Prosecutor that if he does put any questions to the witness relating to that, that we be given extra time in order to analyse this. So we don't know to what document this pertains. Our initial belief was that this involved some medical documentation and this is why we are somewhat taken by surprise now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can deal with the matter quite easily. I can leave this topic to another occasion because they come into two different categories. I needn't go into it in open court. So I can deal with this comment on a later occasion. I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I think that will be the most practical at the moment but could the Chamber further ask of you that you make clear to the members of the Defence what it is that you propose about this document and what its nature and origin is, because that seems to be unknown and obscure at the moment. And with that information, it may be that the Defence will be in a position to cross-examine the witness on the topic during the present session of evidence. I mean by that while the witness is here at this moment. What the Chamber is concerned about is to avoid, if possible, the need for Dr. Bosanac to return at some later time. That would be an unfortunate occurrence if it proved to be necessary. So if that can be avoided, we would like that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, this document quite simply is at the back of the indictment. It is the name of alleged victims. Dr. Bosanac, as indeed my learned friends, looked at this document and was asked if she would be able to recognise the names of any of the individuals and their functions, whether they were civilian, military. Indeed she devised her own category. So this document itself comes from the indictment. It was disclosed to my learned friends. And the categories, S, C, are her categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. So this is not a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All that you are proposing from it is the doctor, from her knowledge of the hospital staff and patients and so forth, to have her identify which patients fell into different possible categories?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Of the list of names that are in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct. The second category of documents, again, my learned friends have not seen that, is basically the patient lists through 1991, clearly targeting, let us say, from June onwards, the names of patients, the nature of the injury, where they were injured, the treatment, and what happened to them, whether they were male, whether they were female. It's something that had not been achievable before we had requested on an RFA for the actual documents so that we could compile our own list. That was not -- we got no reply in relation to that from the authorities. By pure chance I managed to find that there were -- there was a document that was in existence in computer form, which gave those details. We now have those details, but that has only recently arrived. It came with Dr. Bosanac. And I only obtained that myself on Monday. So that has gone to the evidence unit to be collated and has not as yet received an ERN number and has not as yet been looked at with any great detail. So they break into two categories. There document is from the back of the indictment. It relates to the individuals. The other relates to the nature of injuries, the number of people, the extent of injury, whether it be proportionate or disproportionate, which goes, shall I say, to a broader issue, what might be considered the widespread and systematic element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to add something that perhaps could be useful. The Defence does not quite understand whether the list we received from our learned friend represents notes of Mrs. Bosanac based on the computer documentation mentioned by the Prosecutor or whether this is a reflection of her memories, as an aide-memoire, in which case it is not a problem. However, if this was produced on the basis of documentation that has not been processed yet, then in that case, the Defence should be given extra time to prepare for cross-examination and the opportunity to see the documentation used in order to produce this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I can help with regard to it. The list that is in the -- from the back of the indictment was, as far as I'm aware, created from her memory. People that she thought she knew and their specific occupations. In relation to what I will call the computer records, as far as I'm aware, she did not refer to that when she was compiling the list. However, I can clarify it when she is on oath. But that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. The Chamber's view is that the list which you have at your tab 6, which is from the indictment and on which the witness has made, as you understand it from her memory and knowledge, annotations, can be dealt with in the course of her evidence at this moment. It is not really practical for the Chamber to make any ruling in respect of this further information based upon newly acquired computer record until it is available to the Defence and to the Chamber. It is of concern that if you had the document on Monday, we still don't have it. If you would take that firmly on board, Mr. Moore. But that being the case, we would hope that it will be able to be distributed very quickly. That will then enable the Defence to determine whether they need an opportunity to prepare for some questioning on the basis of that document, and it would enable the Chamber to determine whether that request by the Defence was reasonable. We can't do that at the moment, as neither the Defence nor the Chamber has any knowledge. So with respect to the document at tab 6, you may proceed at the moment, and we await the entirely new documents at the earliest opportunity. That I think brings us to a convenient time to adjourn. Mr. Moore, you have something further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it's just one small problem so the Court thinks that we are not being dilatory. The document we have has names and then of course diagnoses. The problem that we have is quite simply this: They are hospital records. The names of the individuals usually can only be released with the permission of the patient. In addition to that, the occupation of the person and the address of the person is on that list as well. Now, it is quite clear that some of those individuals who were on the hospital records were what I will call Croatian defenders or fighters, and there is a clear reluctance by individuals for their names to be disclosed to the Defence. So that is why that that matter has not been dealt with in the way that one normally would do. I can certainly disclose the document immediately with regard to the names being excluded or any identifiable or identifying features. But the problem is, and I cannot give a definitive answer on that, as whether in actual fact any individual who is nominated in a document, where it may strike at their safety, whether in fact one is entitled to disclose such material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What you are saying, Mr. Moore, suggests to me at this moment at least, I've not had a chance to discuss with my other members of the Chamber, that you may find yourself unable to make any use of this further document at all. Or at least, you might only make reference to part of it after there has been some intensive deliberation of issues involving confidentiality, and fairness of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So unless and until we hear more of it, from the Chamber's point of view it will regard it as not a document in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will have to take formal measures to bring it within the trial process and if there are issues of the nature that you indicate, clearly they will have to be formally dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to the hour of 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, would the E-Court throw up the following document number 04637997 -- perhaps "produce" is more attractive than "throw up". And I'd like to refer to the following pages, they are 998, 999, 000, 001, and 002. I, of course, can do it by way of the hard copy method if there is any electronic problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, you had the dubious pleasure of my company last week when I saw you in relation to this case and your evidence. Do you remember being shown this document by the investigator and being asked if you would be able to identify any of the individuals or actually nominate whether -- what they were doing at the hospital? Do you remember that particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we just deal with page 998, please, and if it is possible to highlight the index at the top, which is handwritten. Thank you very much. Doctor, is it correct to say that that is your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what exactly does this represent, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attempted to mark the names, indicating which people I knew and what was the position, what was the role of these people, whether they were medical staff, non-professional staff, whether they were civilians or Croatian soldiers. And what you see in the heading is the key, the legend, where I used the asterisk to mark the hospital workers, then I used the cross to mark the non-professional staff at the hospital. "S" is the symbol I used for wounded soldiers, and then the next category, political enemies or opponents, was the most difficult category because I wasn't quite sure as to who played which role. And then I used letter "C" to denote civilians. We can go name by name and I can tell you what I know about some people. I need to mention once again that I don't know all the people. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, before you do that, I just want to deal with the legend in a little more detail. So if we start at the very top, there is a star and then what seems to be "WH." That is the workers in the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Coming down we have got a cross, perhaps it's -- my copy is rather bad, it seems to be "HW." And then like an "H" again. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Help workers at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So we've got help workers and then we've got what I call ditto. So help workers in the hospital, including civilians and soldiers, is that what you've written down?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The "VS" is soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then a slightly unusual "W," in my language, I suppose, "P," then a cross?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Political opponents. And then "C" for civilians.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now it's not my aim to go through all these individuals. I'm sure you can be asked lots of questions about it. But when it came to putting the marks here, are you absolutely certain in relation to all your marks or are -- how exactly, what was the process that you adopted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain about the ones that I did mark. I placed question marks wherever I was not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to go through this list. It's self-explanatory, I would submit. Would you very quickly like to go through one more time to confirm the marks that you have had -- or the marks that you have made? I don't know if there is a translation problem. Perhaps the question can be asked again. Does the doctor require any more time to look at this list?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not require any more time, but I would like to say that at the bottom of this table, if I may, it says there is a cross and there is a missing person whose remains have not been identified. But that's not consistent with the list. Most of the persons in this list have been identified, their bodies, that is, from the mass grave at Ovcara. So this must be an old list or, rather, an old document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When it came to actually compiling or shall I say ticking the names and assessing who was what, did you have any help when you marked out this category, whether they be soldiers, political opponents, help workers, et cetera, or did you do it by yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, I have no further questions for you on this matter. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you planning to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's -- there was another document as well. There is the peace agreement I think was not tendered as an exhibit and also this document. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have this document at the moment. Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am tendering both for exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Separately, though?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document, which is the marked schedule or annex to the indictment -- Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 30 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would pause a moment, please. Mr. Vasic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In view of the fact that my colleague proposed these two documents separately, I rose on behalf of all three Defence teams to give our position on the agreement that we spoke about. I assume that it is the agreement that we discussed. All of us Defence teams have certain reserves about this document. This is one of the few -- very few documents the authenticity of which the Defence teams are likely to be challenging. We are facing a situation where we have to check the facts in relation to this document. Therefore, the Defence would like to have this document marked for identification in case we find certain facts that are inconsistent, we would then be challenging the authenticity of this document. This is an agreement which the Prosecutor claims was signed in Zagreb, the so-called evacuation agreement. Based on what the Prosecutor has disclosed to the Defence, it appears that five parties were involved in this. The agreement bears three signatures. At the bottom of the agreement itself, where we find the signatures of the JNA representative, the words "JNA" were added by hand, in our submission. That is easily identifiable. As for the signatories of this agreement, at this point in time the Defence would like to say we have serious doubts that it was signed the way my colleague from the Prosecution said it was. The Defence is making an effort to check these facts and will duly be informing both the Trial Chamber and our learned friends from the OTP of the result of our inquiries. Namely, whether we intend to challenge the authenticity of this document or whether we intend to withdraw any doubts that we may have at this time. Therefore, the Defence moves that this document be marked for identification until such time as we have had an opportunity to check the necessary facts in relation to how this agreement was signed. As for the other proposed document, the Defence has no objections. The list that the witness, Mrs. Bosanac marked based on her recollection of events, as she said herself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we will deal first with the list taken from the annex to the indictment. That will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any submission about the proposal that the agreement which you have been referring to should now be marked for identification rather than exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. We accept that the Defence are entitled to check the authenticity and would make no objection at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The agreement document, which has been referred to in the course of evidence, will be now marked for identification. The number of that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would be number 40, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've got the document now electronically?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore, anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, Defence counsel will now, I expect, want to ask you some questions. I turn first to Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be the first to cross-examine the witness on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wish to introduce myself first of all, I'm Miroslav Vasic, first of all, appearing on behalf of Mile Mrksic. We speak the same language. Therefore I would like to ask you to please make a short break after my questions so that the interpreters can accurately interpret the proceedings, in order to allow everybody else in the courtroom to follow our exchange. Yesterday, when answering a question by my learned friend, you said you became manager of the medical centre in Vukovar on the 25th of July 1991. Were you appointed after the previous manager, a Serb, had resigned facing pressure from the Croatian health ministry?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous manager, Dr. Rade Popovic, a neuropsychiatrist, resigned. He was from Montenegro, as a matter of fact. He resigned. I'm not sure about the reasons why he did so, but he resigned. I was a member of the employees' council and I was appointed acting director by vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Bosanac. Do you know whether in May 1991 a new manager was appointed to Radio Vukovar, a Croat replacing a Serb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who was the manager and when, but I remember I listened to the radio and the information was that Professor Lenjak had become manager of Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While listening to the radio, did you perhaps hear that in May 1991, Radio Vukovar changed its name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when that occurred. I know that it was now called Croatian Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to deal now with the background of what preceded the events you testified about during the examination-in-chief. You're an intellectual and you must be aware of the fact that after the multi-party elections in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia in 1990 which resulted in an HDZ victory, the constitution of the Republic of Croatia was changed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell me whether these changes in the constitution changed the constitutional position of Serbs in Croatia, in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I did not study the constitution that closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the results of the elections were in 1990 in Vukovar municipality? Who won?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly but I know that the local elections took place in the spring of 1991. That's in fact what I believe. It was not in 1990, as you stated. I can't talk about the specific percentages but I know that several parties entered the municipality and that Slavko Dokmanovic became president of municipality, while Mr. Soldo was president of the executive committee. These are things that I remember but I can't give you the exact results.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which party Slavko Dokmanovic was a member of?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure about this but I think it was a Communist Party, just that I can't remember which one. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was Ivica Racan perhaps the president of that party for all of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that there was a split in the Communist Party at the time, one faction being in favour of Croatia, the other in favour of Yugoslavia. But I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know for how long Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic remained president of Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of exact dates but I know it was after the notorious occurrences in Borovo Selo when 12 Croatian police officers were killed. Tensions began to mount and some roadblocks had already been set up. I remember watching Novi Sad television. Mr. Dokmanovic was there, whether in Trpinja -- he was from Trpinja but I can't remember it was Trpinja or not. He was from one of those villages and he was explaining to the viewers why he was not able to go to work. I'm not sure whether it was June or July. I just know what I heard. Mr. Dokmanovic was unable to go to work in Vukovar and the Croatian government appointed an acting president, Mr. Marin Vidic, also known as Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was an ethnic Serb, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. But I don't know. I did not know Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the commissioner appointed by the Croatian government? What ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat. Marin Vidic. He was from Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know which party the commissioner belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If, as you said, Slavko Dokmanovic was supposed to reach Vukovar through Trpinja would he have had to go through Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could have taken a roundabout route but the one you have just suggested was certainly the shortest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know anyone named Blago Zadro?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In January 1991, was this person president of the executive committee of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know anyone named Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In January 1991, was he president of the municipal committee, the municipal HDZ committee for Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps the secretary of the secretariat for All People's Defence for Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in July in Borovo Selo, a cleansing operation had been carried out to cleanse the northern sector of Borovo Naselje. This was something conducted by the HDA [as interpreted] in order to expel the ethnic Serbs from that village?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the situation at the Vukovar police station in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Stipo Pole was chief of the police station. For a while, the post was held by someone I didn't know. Whether he was killed in Borovo Selo or whether the change was caused by something else, I don't know. But in the summer of 1991, when I became hospital manager, Stipo Pole was chief of the Vukovar police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the spring of 1991, Serb members of the Vukovar police station were fired and that a large number of Croat reserve police officers were brought in as replacements?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 2nd of May events in Borovo Selo. Can you tell us whether, after what happened there, wounded Croatian police officers were brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that an ambulance from the Vukovar medical centre was sent out. I was not part of the hospital management at the time. I'm not sure who was in charge. I know that some people had been killed and that the wounded had been brought in, and then taken elsewhere by helicopter. I'm unable to provide any details, though. At the time, I worked at a specialist medical station. I conducted medical examinations of children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you were, after all, working at the hospital, weren't you. In view of that fact, did you know that the ethnic makeup of those employed by the hospital actually changed between May and July, at the expense of Serbs? Isn't it true that ethnic Serbs were leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that many of them no longer came to work. They left the hospital. They no longer came to work. They were probably using their annual leave and whatever days off they had. I saw them on Serbian television, that they were setting up a war hospital in Bobota, some of them at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You did not speak to any of the Serbs working in the hospital at the time? You didn't speak to them about why they were leaving, whether perhaps they were afraid of something?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not speak to any of them. I was on duty one night with a nurse from Negoslavci. Her husband phoned and told her to go home immediately because they were taking their children to Sid. She was taken aback. She said she would not allow her children to go anywhere and that she was unable to leave work. She was shocked and surprised. My impression was that she was really taken aback. However, the next day she did not turn up for work. In my opinion, this is something that was organised. People were taking their children to Serbia. I also had some patients from Borovo Selo. Their mothers had said that they would like to come and visit the hospital but that they were not allowed to go. Rather, they were being sent by boat across to Backa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the 2nd of May, was a Crisis Staff established at the hospital? And was the task of this Crisis Staff to prepare the hospital for an emergency? Was, in fact, a state of emergency declared?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what happened after the 2nd of May. I can tell you what happened after I was appointed manager of the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you in fact a member of this staff at one point in time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the person who set it up. I really don't know whether there had been a staff before I came along.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time, were there any soldiers in the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But there were no armed clashes at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were soldiers in the barracks, military vehicles drove through the town and a daily basis on their way to Borovo Selo and back. Armoured military vehicles were passing to and through.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the spring of 1991, Serb houses were torched and demolished in Vukovar and the Borba media company kiosk was in fact bombed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly when I heard this but I did hear that some of the pubs or bars were blown up. The rumour was that the owners themselves had planted the explosive in order to collect the insurance money, but it wasn't really certain who had done that. One thing I'd like to point out is that the armed clashes in Vukovar started after 12 Croatian police officers had been killed in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that there were -- was some combat activity immediately following the 2nd of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, in one of your questions, you said during the summer, when there was still no conflicts. And what I was trying to say is, is that the conflict actually broke out when those policemen were killed. In July, the first shells started landing on Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the following names: Vlada Skeledzija, Branko Mirijanic [phoen], Mladen Mirkic? They were from Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at one point in time the barracks in Vukovar was placed under siege by the members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 3rd of September 1991, upon orders of the commissioner, the water supply was cut off for the barracks as well as electricity, following which there was an armed attack on the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the municipal Crisis Staff in Vukovar was founded?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but I think that was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who were members of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was led by the government commissioner, Mr. Marin Vidic. In addition to him, there were people from civilian protection, from the water works company, and so on. I know that the person representing the hospital on the staff was Dr. Matos.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there any military commanders or MUP commanders on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend those meetings regularly. And I'm not sure how this Crisis Staff functioned. I know I went several times, once or twice, to attend the meetings. Then I saw Mr. Polet, a representative of the police force, but I saw no military representatives. That was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the people you mentioned were also members of the HDZ, in addition to being members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not. I don't know nor a fact but I don't think that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come that you, as hospital director, were not a member of the Crisis Staff? How come that another doctor from the hospital was on the staff but not you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to deal with various organisational issues, and to go to the meetings was something that somebody else could do and come back and brief us at the hospital. Therefore, Dr. Matos was designated as the go between the hospital and the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
