utterances.text: Was there also a war hospital within the Vukovar medical centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, in view of the situation that developed in the following months, it turned into a war hospital, but it did not exist as a separate unit within the Vukovar medical centre. What happened was that practically the entire hospital, starting in late August until late November when it was occupied, functioned as a war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Dr. Njavro Djuro was in charge of the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was designated by the main medical staff in Zagreb as chief of war surgery because he happened to be a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In examination-in-chief, we saw that, according to your words, you applied to all relevant highest authorities in the Republic of Croatia who did nothing to change the difficult situation in which the hospital found itself. Was there somebody else perhaps who was better placed than you to address such requests to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was another person other than me. I wasn't the only one who sent out faxes and asked for help. A lot of us did that. Dr. Njavro, myself, Marin Vidic. Croatian Radio Vukovar kept issuing calls for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Dr. Matos who was a member of the Crisis Staff, did he perhaps have greater power when it comes to the dealings with the authorities of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Matos was the liaison between the hospital and the municipal Crisis Staff. Therefore, I do not think that he had greater power or greater authority, if this is what you prefer, to ensure that the Vukovar Hospital got more help. It was absolutely impossible, in view of the weapons that the JNA had brought to Vukovar. Not a bird could fly through, let alone eight convoys. There with were so many planes flying over and so many shells and bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict, were there any helicopters that flew between the rest of Croatia and Vukovar, and were there any helicopters landing at the stadium near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Didn't you propose, in one of your calls for help, that the assistance for the hospital be provided in that way, because that was the only viable option?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I did. I proposed all kinds of options, but there was no chance for a helicopter to get there without being shot by the JNA artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you, as hospital director, appointed a doctor to serve as a liaison with the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean the military formation. Was there a doctor who was a liaison with them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke about the artillery firing, multi-barrelled rocket launchers firing from the left bank of the Danube and you were able to see them. Can you please tell us whether these tanks and multi-barrel rocket launchers were located in Backa which is in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that these units were outside of the territory of Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is still a contentious issue. I personally believe that the border runs through Bend and that on the left bank of the Danube, where I personally saw tanks, that that part is still considered the territory of the former municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As I see it, that's on the north side of Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on the left bank of the Danube, directly across the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your testimony, you said that the planes attacked Mitnica even though there was no combat activity there. Don't you know that on the 18th of November, Mitnica battalion, which was part of the National Guards Corps, surrendered? It was part of the National Guards Corps of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that on the 18th of November, some of the members of the National Guards Corps, led by Filip Karaula surrendered. However, yesterday in my testimony, I did not mention that Mitnica was a civilian settlement and that there was not a single military target that could be bombed by planes. As far as I know, members of the National Guards Corps held borderline positions towards the area where the siege was laid, siege of Vukovar. The planes destructed everything, schools, hospital, just about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I apologise. I have to interrupt you and ask you this. Wasn't this the last stronghold of the National Guards Corps that remained there until the 18th of November? So can we agree on this, that the stronghold of the National Guards Corps is a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that that was the National Guards Corps stronghold because there was not a single military facility there which could have housed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know something about the course of the combat in Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what I heard. I never personally went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, when you were asked by my learned friend, you said that the members of the JNA reached the hospital for the first time on the 19th of November 1991. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also said that an officer came with two soldiers and took you to Negoslavci. Did this officer enter the hospital building in the morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to the reception desk of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On the previous day, on the 18th, in the presence of a JNA officer, did you speak in the hospital with General Antun Tus, accusing him of not sending aid and saying that that was the cause of the fall of Vukovar and that it was too late to send any kind of assistance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the National Guards Corps, in the last days of combat, killed -- killed people and threw them out of the hospital in order to make space for them there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. At least not while I was at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you at least hear such stories?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that weapons were found at the hospital, discarded by the members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that for the first time in prison, when I was interrogated about whether there were any weapons in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in Negoslavci, did Colonel Mrksic thank you for treating soldier Jovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Mrksic send food and water to the hospital which arrived approximately at the same time when you returned from Negoslavci to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that during those last days, the 17th, 18th, and 19th, civilians started arriving in the hospital, because they knew there would be an evacuation. How were they able to know that, if they, as you told us, stayed continuously in shelters and basements? How were they able then to acquire such information?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably heard it from each other, heard that an evacuation was being prepared. People knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The flow of the wounded, did that subside after the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the wounded who were members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the wounded did decrease. The last major intake was on the 15th of November, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Members of the Guards and MUP who were withdrawing from other parts of the town, were they all moving in the direction of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the National Guards Corps and police force in those days, upon piercing and breaking the siege, were actually leaving Vukovar. Only the wounded were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you are trying to say is that the majority of ZNG members and police force left Vukovar despite this siege?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the majority of them managed to flee Vukovar, but I know that following these operations a lot of them ended up in prisons throughout Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The entire command structure, including the commander of Vukovar defence, Mile Dedakovic and the second commander, Borkovic, did they all leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when asked by my learned friend, you said you were concerned about what was going to happen once the military reached the hospital, and do you know that one of the main conditions for the Mitnica battalion to surrender was the condition that it surrender to the military?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we know that the Mitnica Battalion surrendered in Mitnica, that the command structure of the National Guards Corps and MUP had left Vukovar, can you tell us what happened to their other members? Did they perhaps seek shelter in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't say. I don't know who you have in mind. They did not seek shelter in the hospital. Most of them tried to break through. They were making attempts to break through, for several nights in a row, just before the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This breakthrough, was that a form of armed combat or do you just mean getting through?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean just getting through. They didn't know what lay in store for them but they broke out anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore it seems that the blockade was not as tight as you suggested to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very tight when humanitarian aid was supposed to arrive. Still, many people managed to leave, many of them were captured and spent months in prisons in Serbia. Many of them were killed, and are still listed as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned humanitarian aid missions. Can you confirm that a Medecins Sans Frontieres convoy that evacuated the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th of December, in fact -- the 18th of October, in fact deviated from the route that had been agreed with the Croatian National Guards corps commander in Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't speak about that. I wasn't part of the convoy myself. I know that the convoy was derailed, as it were, and that it spent the next night and day travelling over muddy fields and coming across a minefield. I know nothing else because I wasn't part of the convoy myself, nor did I have any other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the convoy that was supposed to arrive on the 13th of October, and which eventually made it to the Vukovar barracks? Do you know that they couldn't get through to the hospital because the ZNG, National Guards Corps, and MUP command refused to allow them to get through?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it eventually failed to get through, but I know that they were carrying a lot of medical equipment and medicine that they were made to unload in the barracks and go back without a single pill and a single drip. That's one thing that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the list of the wounded people who arrived in the hospital was made? Did you use notebooks for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were files, documents, kept in the following way. Any admission would be registered, the wounded, the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that in fact a notebook that was being used to record these details?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not a notebook, really. There is the register book. It's actually quite big and it's usually kept on the table of the medical centre of the clinic. Information was entered into this register book on the state of the patient, on what sort of surgery a patient undergoes, specialists were typewritten and compiled of patients wounded that were then sent to the health ministry, to the police headquarters, to the Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In these register books, in addition to the first and last name of a patient, was their status also reflected?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the register book but the lists that were sent, that were passed on to the ministry, always clearly stated whether somebody was a member of the National Guards Corps or a civilian, a child or a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know someone named Branko Stankovic? He was a patient at your hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, have an overview of all the patients being admitted into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But you do not remember this particular patient or are you saying that he was never admitted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Toma Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what became of him before combat operations ceased in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in prison, when I was being interrogated, I know what happened when he was wounded, when he was in the hospital, and then we sent him to Komerc. This is something that I heard in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That he was killed there, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that his dead body was found. I don't know how or when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what became of the following soldiers, Slavmir Destir [phoen], and Milan Biber who were admitted into the hospital on the 20th of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mean you don't remember or are you saying that they were not admitted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names of the soldiers who were killed or wounded when they came across some mines on the Borovo road. I think one of them was called Slaven [phoen] but I can't be certain. If these are the people you're talking about, these soldiers who were wounded at that time, they were brought in a van for lack of an ambulance, of course, to the barracks occupied by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In relation to these soldiers, there is no information indicating that they were taken anywhere, in fact. They are listed as missing in the military files. This is not something that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Nedeljko Turekalo, admitted on the 30th of October 1991, to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. I can't remember that he was ever brought in, and I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a wounded soldier named Ivan Zivkovic who was in the hospital and who joined the convoy that left Vukovar on the 18th of October?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember every single name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about the special treatment awarded soldiers such as Sasa Jovic, that they were being guarded by the National Guards Corps and being treated by Dr. Njavro. Did you assign Dr. Njavro to treat these patients, or was he assigned by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro was the chief surgeon of the hospital. He him self decided to treat them, to treat them alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps police had a special interest in these people, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were worrying, they were making phone calls to inquire about their situation. That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were they in fact being guarded by a member of the National Guards Corps called Damjan Samardzic, also known as The Big Bojler?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the person who was assigned. He was watching them and that must be one of the reasons they killed him at Ovcara even before they shot everybody else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My apologies, the name of Damjan Samardzic was not recorded in the transcript. Can you tell us when it was that Mile Dedakovic, the Vukovar Defence commander, left Vukovar? Do you know the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. It was in early October. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did you get to meet the new commander, Borkovic, also known as Mladi Jastreb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in early September, when Mile Dedakovic appointed Borkovic as coordinator for civilian protection and for the municipal Crisis Staff. That was the first time I saw him. Later on, I used to see him at the headquarters whenever I went there to send faxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While Borkovic was commander of the Vukovar defence, did he not in fact disconnect your phone lines, the hospital phone lines, connecting you to the outer world?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said 10 days earlier that there would be a blockade, an information blockade to prevent information from reaching anyone outside. My phone lines were operational all the way to the very end, which I used to send out my appeals. And the same applied to Radio Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he not in fact do the same thing to the Crisis Staff? Did he not disconnect their lines, cut off their lines of communication?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did about the Crisis Staff, but I know that I myself was sending these faxes throughout all the way until the 15th of November. If you go back to the documents, you can check the dates and see for how long I continued to send out these appeals by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that for a while you were using a phone that was not in the hospital in order to send your messages, a phone that was located else where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the hospital telephone but I used the fax machine which was in the Defence Staff building and the police building. That's until the time that the police building was destroyed. But I had the phone throughout. The first time I was unable to talk was on the 20th, in the morning, when I was brought back to the hospital from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement mentioned yesterday by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, the statement that you gave the security bodies while you were in prison, Colonel Branko, more specifically, did you not say that Borkovic had cut off your communication lines as well as those of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly what I stated on that occasion. I do know that he said he would impose an information ban on all information leaving Vukovar. That was 10 days before the fall of Vukovar. I took this to be a sign of his desperation, of his helplessness, his inability to do anything about it. But as I've already said I was able to physically use the phone on all days until the 20th. Most of the other phone lines had been demolished and you couldn't call just anyone you liked. You couldn't just call outside whenever and whoever you wanted to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You spoke today about categories of persons and the markings that you made pursuant to a request by the Prosecutor. I'm talking about the list that was tendered today. There is a category there defined as help worker at the hospital. Can you please specify what that means?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were persons helping out at the hospital, auxiliaries working as butchers, storage people, porters. They were carrying water.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether that category includes civilians and soldiers also?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was about to say. There were persons who had been tasked with a security detail by the Defence Staff and they were at the hospital as security. There were people from the police who were in charge of collecting weapons, identifying dead bodies and sending lists off to the police. That is why I defined the category as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who was it who defined this category? Who had the authority to say who was and who was not a helping worker, help worker?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence commander sent certain people to the hospital to help out and to provide security. So did the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A while ago we mentioned Colonel Branko who you gave your statement to. Can you describe his physical appearance, if you still remember what he looks like?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult. Not very small, not very tall. Say, medium build, dark hair. Balding slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in a position to see a letter of protest which reads indictment, and was in fact sent to the leaders of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where the government of the Republic of Croatia is accused of having betrayed Vukovar? Perhaps you would like some water.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm thinking about what indictment and what letter you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see a letter of protest entitled "indictment" or "accusation" sent by the Crisis Staff to the Croatian government accusing them of having betrayed Vukovar and its defenders as well as its people?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I actually saw parts of that letter, after I was released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please go into private session for a moment? I would like to ask the witness some questions in reference to witnesses who have been granted protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that between 80 and 90 shells, bombs and missiles hit the hospital daily. This means that from the 15th of August to mid-November, that would come up to between 6 and 7.000 various shells, and over 40.000 kilograms of explosives. Don't you think that, in view of these figures, and this amount, the hospital should be completely razed to the ground and we would not be able to see the footage that we saw when you were examined in chief by our learned friend?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated about the facts that I'm sure of, and that I knew about. I didn't count bombs, shells, and all other ordnance every day. I don't know whether you ever visited Vukovar after the 20th of November. Had you visited it, then you would have known that that was true. This is what landed on the hospital, and hundred times more various ordnance landed on the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions, as we have agreement among us Defence counsel not to overlap in our questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The witness said in fact that she did count the ordnance that fell on the hospital, not "did not count," as is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you hear that last correction, Mr. Vasic? It wouldn't have troubled you. It only troubled those who were hearing an English-language interpretation. You would have heard the answer in B/C/S. Thank you, Mr. Vasic. I think probably this is a convenient time to break, and we can continue cross-examination after the break. We will resume at 20 minutes to one. That's at 12.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one matter I'd like the Court's guidance on, please. We have just had served on us some documents by the Defence that are going to be used in cross-examination. Well, of course, I don't in any way criticise the Defence ability to cross-examine on documents, but with the utmost respect, in fairness to the Prosecution in this instance, it would have been helpful if we have at least see the documents so we have a chance to read them, assimilate them and to mount an objection if it's necessary. We have always given the Defence the documents that we intend to rely upon; they have had opportunities to do so. My understanding is that people have got to be even-handed. I understand Mr. Lukic's point about surprise but nevertheless this is not surprise. This is disadvantage. And that in my submission is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, without calling on the Defence, there is a fundamental distinction; that is the Prosecution has an obligation to disclose all relevant documents for and against its case to the Defence. Under the more traditional view of disclosure by the Defence, there is no equivalent obligation on the Defence. And that, of course, is what was at the point of this issue which was debated and decided yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that is about disclosure. It is well-recognised that an unsatisfactory consequence of the traditional view is that documents may be produced of which the Prosecution has no familiarity and which they must, on the run, as it were, decide whether the document can be the subject of valid objection and, even more problematic, whether they will be in a position to deal effectively with that document in re-examination, when the time comes. Because of that unsatisfactory element, as I indicated yesterday, some jurisdictions in the world are gradually changing to some degree from the traditional rigid position so as to enable the trial to run more smoothly and to enable counsel to be in a better position to deal with issues as they arise. It's often said in shorthand it's not in the interests of justice for there to be trial by ambush, and in a sense, this traditional position enables trial by ambush. We are well aware of all of that, but if the Defence feels it has reason not to disclose a document, unless we see from a pattern of conduct that that is being unnecessarily abused, we, at the moment, take the position that the traditional position, which has prevailed long in this Tribunal, should continue in this trial. A consequence is, unfortunately for the length of the trial, that you may need to seek to delay re-examination, you may have to make objections to a document which, had you been more fully prepared, would you not have needed to do so. Those things may happen. And it also may mean that you may have to seek a delay in your re-examination. You may even need to mount a submission for leave to call evidence in rebuttal. All of that prolonging may be a consequence of what can occur. There is nothing knew about that in this trial. It's typical of trials in this Tribunal, and under the traditional adversarial system. In the interests of the speed and efficiency of this trial, which the accused have more interest in than anybody else because I'm sure the sooner they can get this trial concluded and know exactly where they stand, the better it is for them. In the interests of that, we would very much encourage Defence counsel at this stage, unless they have particular reason with a particular document, to have common sense and courtesy, and try and allow the Prosecution to have some advance knowledge of the documents they may intend to use, both in cross-examination and when the Defence comes to be presenting their respective cases. If that can be done, for the most part, we can minimise unnecessary delay, unnecessary adjournment, unnecessary need to recall witnesses, and so on. What I have said, though, I trust it would remain clear that at the moment the Chamber is prepared to recognise and respect that Defence counsel may have particular reason, with a particular document, to want to deal with it without notice. As long as that isn't being abused, the present position of the Chamber is, as indicated yesterday, that it will not interfere with that way of conducting the Defence case. But as indicated yesterday, we will be keeping the position under review and we may come back as the practice direction and the rules allow, to requiring an earlier notice of all documents, if the position is not handled sensibly and responsibly. Now, I trust those impromptu comments will make clear the Chamber's understanding and appreciation of the position and that we are constantly watching how this is handled by counsel, and while I've been speaking of Prosecution and Defence, at the moment I'm doing so in the context of the Prosecution case. The reverse applies when the Defence is presenting its case equally. So, Mr. Moore, the answer is we are sorry and concerned that you have just got a bundle of documents. It may be a position aggravated at the moment because of the earliness of the trial and the complications of getting documents ordered with the change of plan with regard to the electronic court system. I would hope that the Prosecution will find that as the trial progresses you will have reasonable notice of the majority, if not all of documents that will be used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Mr. Borovic representing Miroslav Radic. I said this with the benefit of the witness. Before I begin my cross-examination I need to give an explanation to the Trial Chamber. And I would ask the president of the Trial Chamber to give an instruction to the Defence. We said today that we received last night the documents that were promised to us by the approximate several days ago. We received it yesterday with the translation and, in the future, this ought to be done in accordance with instructions received from the Trial Chamber and in the -- in accordance with the agreement we made yesterday. In order to be sure that we all interpret the instructions in the same way, I would like to know whether, on occasion, I would be able to use the statements of witnesses who have not yet testified in trial. I am not saying that that would be my motive, to do that, to have them admitted in advance, but, since all of these documents have been disclosed to us, what we would like to do is to present certain documents when examining witnesses. This is needed in order for -- in order to achieve trial efficiency and to ensure fair proceedings and, since we have the witness before us here today, we think it would be wise to present certain documents to this witness in order to avoid any waste of time in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, for the purposes of cross-examination, you would not normally be able to tender, for example, the statement of a witness who had not yet given evidence, as part of your case. You may well, however, having read a statement that's been provided to you of evidence that is expected to be given by a witness, you may well want to put to a witness now giving evidence questions to see whether that witness agrees with what you understand will be said in the future or disagrees with it. You can do that normally without having need to show the witness the actual statement. You simply say, "If a witness were to say this or that, is that something you agree with?" Or "you know very well Mr. Smith. Would it surprise you to learn that Mr. Smith has made a statement indicating that things happened very differently from what you have said? And he said this or that." I just use those as simple illustrations of the way you may test with a present witness evidence that may arise at some future time. Separately from that, there may be times where a particular document which has been disclosed to you by the Prosecution in its disclosure, or which you have and you believe to be an authentic document, and which appears to be contrary to evidence that's being given by a present witness, you may well want or need to put that actual document to the witness and say, "Now, this document appears to contradict what you're saying," or whatever it may be and get the witness's reaction to the document. In that case, unless the Prosecution agrees to the document then becoming evidence, you would need to have the document marked for identification and at some later time, you would need yourself to prove that document in evidence by some proper means. If it's a document which is going to be presented by some future Prosecution witness, when that future Prosecution witness is giving evidence, you in your cross-examination might put that document to that witness, have the witness identify and authenticate the document, and then it could be transferred from merely being marked for identification to becoming an exhibit. Is that a sufficient indication for you of where the Chamber sees the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is more than sufficient. I'm very grateful to you for your instructions. In order not to waste any time in the future, I asked for this instruction to be given to us now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm merely outlining to you the law relevant to admissibility in cross-examination, the general law, at least as I understand it. I would suggest that you and all other counsel might use that as a basis for your approach to questioning and the use of documents in cross-examination. If you have a particular problem, of course, you may always raise that with the Chamber. But you can treat that as an indication of our general position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall begin with my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with one of the questions already asked by my colleague, Mr. Vasic. The first question was whether Mr. Rade Popovic resigned as hospital manager as the witness stated or was he in fact removed from that position? My question is: Does the witness know Binazija Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was she employed by the hospital? Was she working at the hospital during these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Binazija Kolesar, according to a statement she gave the OTP, which my learned friend can no doubt confirm, on the 20th of June 1995, page 2, paragraph 2, states that the manager of the Vukovar general hospital before Dr. Vesna Bosanac was Dr. Rade Popovic, and he was removed from his post in 1991. I move that these documents be made evidence and can the usher please distribute to all participants, as well as to the witness, evidence from tab 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They can be distributed at the moment for the purposes of examining. We'll look at the question of whether they should be evidence a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We would object to that course. If it's the document that my learned friend is referring to, which is dated the 18th of July, the correct procedure, in my submission, is for the doctor to look at this document to ascertain whether she has seen the document before, has any knowledge of the document or created the document, if she does not know of the document, in my submission, she should not be then asked any questions in relation to it. It may well be that this document can be adduced as evidence as part of the Defence case but a witness in my submission, if they say they don't know the document, or to what it relates, in my submission, is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I think we are in firm agreement. You misunderstood the purport I have said. It can be distributed now so that it's in the hands of parties, as Mr. Borovic then puts the document to the witness. I said we would look later at the question of whether or not it should be admitted in evidence. And that will be determined in part on the witness's reaction to the document and what she knows of it. Is that clear enough, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crystal clear, Your Honour. I expected that once I've asked my questions, the Prosecutor would be reacting, which they did with no delay. I'm now preparing to have the document distributed to the witness and to ask her questions about the document, and about Kolesar Binazija's statement which I have just quoted. .

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My first question therefore: Is it true what Kolesar Binazija is saying here, namely that Dr. Popovic was in fact removed from his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect I object to that. Kolesar's statement does not say that. It says "replaced," not "removed."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, this is in fact precisely what the statement says, that the manager of the general hospital before Dr. Vesna Bosanac was Dr. Rade Popovic who was removed in 1991. This is not the same as resigning from your post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, we are getting tied up with the document. The question you put was not related to the document at all. It was simply asking the doctor whether Dr. Popovic was removed in 1991. And you haven't yet had an answer to that. When you get an answer to that from the witness's knowledge, you may then want to say, if you have a document that is contradicting that, you may want to show the witness the document and ask the witness whether she recognises the document, whether she agrees with its content, if it says something different from what you are putting to the witness. Is that helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whatever you say is helpful. Needless to say. But I closely followed the questions of my colleague, Mr. Vasic. In answer to the same question, the witness insisted that Dr. Popovic resigned of his own free will and this is why I'm trying to ask the question in a different way by showing the witness this statement which claims that he did not in fact resign but rather was removed from his post. I'm trying to show the witness this document. Therefore, I will try to re-ask this same question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're not only re-asking the question. You're wanting now to have the witness examine this document and see whether that changes her mind. Is that what you're wanting to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, yes. That is precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. And is the document the first document in the bundle that you've provided? A letter of the 1st of December 1991? Or is it some other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I enclosed a document dated the 18th of July 1991. This is a request for dismissal by the justice ministry. It's in tab 1, as I have stated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was misled by the endorsement that's up at the top right-hand corner in handwriting. It's -- the date of the document is the 18th of July 1991. Now, I believe that Dr. Bosanac has that, a copy of that in front of her. Do you recognise the document at all, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, could you direct the doctor's attention, please, Mr. Borovic, to the particular paragraph that you're concerned with?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll start with the bit where it says, "Subject," request for the removal of or dismissal of director, Dr. Rade Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Was this a request by the ministry prompted by the doctor's proposal to resign or was there a different reason behind this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will first answer your first question. Do you want me to answer your first question about Binazija Kolesar or the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Perhaps you should start by answering the first question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my previous statement. Dr. Rade Popovic resigned of his own free will from his post as manager of the Vukovar general hospital. I was present at the meeting of the workers council when he handed in his resignation. Binazija Kolesar was not an employee of the hospital administration at the time. What she stated was perhaps based on hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness now please answer the second question?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this letter, sent by the health ministry on the 18th of July 1991 to the chairman of the workers' council, was sent after the dismissal request -- whether Dr. Popovic himself handed in a request to resign or not. This is something that I don't know. It was only after I was myself appointed manager of the hospital, or, rather, acting manager, that I first laid eyes on this document. In as far as that is relevant to the Court, perhaps it would be a good idea to call Rade Popovic such himself to testify. He still works at the Vukovar Hospital. And a correction, if I may, he did not resign from the hospital altogether. He just resigned from his post as manager but he continued to work as a neuropsychiatrist within the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Binazija Kolesar, a witness who appeared quite decided in her statement when saying that he was dismissed and had not in fact resigned, is not speaking the truth?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I was there when he handed in his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what would be your answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is I was physically present at this meeting where he handed in his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But I asked you whether Binazija Kolesar was speaking the truth or are you speaking the truth?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that I am the one speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question by my learned friend Mr. Vasic whether explosives were laid to Serb shops, we heard the witness say that she was familiar with one particular case where the Serbs laid explosives to their own shop in order to collect the insurance. My question to the witness in relation to this incident is: Does the witness in fact know who is -- who Delika Mirsic [phoen] is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this a person that the witness mentioned in her previous statements to various military and judicial authorities?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In Sremska Mitrovica, did the witness give a statement referred to by the Prosecutor today? Did she give many statements or just this one that was mentioned by the Prosecutor during his examination?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my captivity in Sremska Mitrovica and Belgrade, I gave a written statement concerning a number of different situations, both before and during the war in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My specific question is: The statement that was referred to by the Prosecutor today, given by the witness during her captivity in the Sremska Mitrovica prison, her detention, she confirmed that she did indeed give this statement and signed it -- sign it, she certainly not happy that she was in prison there but she certainly stated that she was there in prison. I would now like to read a portion of the statement which has a heading. We will have this shown if necessary and I think the Prosecutor can confirm that this is the very statement, because they quoted the statement today. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, could you show a copy of the document to the witness, and the witness, I would expect, would know better than anybody whether it was the statement she made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The first question is: Is this the statement that the witness herself wrote?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that this is the statement that I wrote in prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In future, sir, please, if you would be so kind to allow me to finish my sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: By all means. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wish to say I confirm that to the extent that I can see this is indeed my handwriting, and a portion of the statement that I wrote while I was in detention in Sremska Mitrovica. There is one thing that I wish to point out to the Trial Chamber, however. I wrote this statement in detention, and under duress. I was being guided and instructed as to what I was supposed to write and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I have not tendered this document in my capacity as Defence counsel. I'm merely showing a statement which you have just confirmed that you wrote and signed. Can the witness please read out this portion that I have now shown, just below the heading, "The mining and torching of cafes owned by Serbs," whether this will in fact be tendered into evidence and what the probative value of the document might have is something that the Court will determine later on. Can you just please read the first portion of --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first portion of the page, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted her to read out the bit where it says "the mining and torching of Serb-owned cafes." This statement runs into dozens of pages and that is one reason why I am not yet tendering it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying again that I wrote this statement under duress, in detention. I was being guided and instructed as to what and how I was supposed to write. Whether I heard that Serb-owned cafes and houses were being torched in Vukovar, the heading itself, too, was dictated to me by the interrogator. "The torching and mining of Serb-owned cafes" ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please continue reading the text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a document we have a copy of in this bundle, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The reason is I will not be tendering this document into evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're wanting us to appreciate what is there written, it would be appropriate in all future cases to have copies available for the Chamber, if you're putting a paper document to the witness. I take it, Mr. Moore, you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have an English translation, but I don't know to which part my learned friend is referring. I suspect it may be on the English version 1224 on the hard copy but I suspect the problem will arise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on for the moment, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, over your shoulder I see Mr. Lukic trying to get a word in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be of assistance, both to the Chamber and the rest of the parties in the courtroom. My team has prepared this document to be tendered in -- when we conduct our cross-examination. It is ready, and even though it is not our turn yet, I think that it is ready now. The entire document has about 160 pages, together with an English translation, and our team has prepared that in the electronic version. Perhaps that could be done now through the Registrar so that we can use this document now when my colleague, Mr. Borovic, is questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. I think that will be of assistance to Mr. Borovic and to the Chamber, so that we will be able to follow what is being put. Hopefully it will be able to be turned up in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence teams have divided among them various documents to be tendered during their bits of cross-examination or examination, and this is what the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin has told us. The numbers are 3D 00-001 for the B/C/S version and 3D 00-0126 is the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Borovic. We have overcome some parts of the technical issues. Please continue. Now, what we do need to be guided to is where in the English-language version we will find the passage you are referring to. Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, it's somewhere in the middle of the text. There is a subheading, "The cafes are being set on fire and blown up." It's on page 107 of the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, are you able to convert to the English text?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If the Court turns to the hard copy for a moment and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I have it on my number, ERN number, and I have a copy here which is Y0041224. That is the number that I have and the subtext that I think it may relate to is how a cafe owned by Serbs was torched and blown up. So the number is Y0041224. I believe that may be the section but I don't speak B/C/S, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will look at page 54 and 55 and see -- just doing a quick lot of mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to be of assistance. Page 55 of the English version, number 3D 00-0180. The text is -- the relevant portion is somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In the interests of justice, I have to be patient and persistent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please read the text.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be shown on my monitor, please? I would like to see what you are seeing on your monitors because on my monitor I only have the first page of the said statement. I want to be sure that you can follow and check what I'm reading. Or do you want me to reply regardless?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the page number in the B/C/S version, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 107. And this is precisely the page we gave to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have in front of me is page 9, 109. I ask that the English translation of this page be shown on the monitor so that I can compare the two to make sure that that is precisely the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you read a heading, "How a cafe owned by Serbs was torched and blown up" on the page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can be of assistance here. I have another copy of the B/C/S version. There is a single subheading there. You have the same page on your screens. And could this please be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it on my screen now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you're asking the witness to read this to herself before you ask questions or do you want her to read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask her to read it out loud because previously she stated, loud and clear, she didn't know Darko Markobasic, and from this portion here you will see how things actually lie. This is something written in the handwriting of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, but prior to this, I would like to state that I did not reply to the question put by Defence about Marko -- Darko Markobasic and I didn't say that I didn't know him. I said that I knew him. Whereas what I actually said was, when asked by you, that I did not say so in any statements I have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bosanac. Now, could you please read the text?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I, as well as many other citizens, were unpleasantly surprised upon learning that every four or five days a Serbian restaurant is blown up. The Borba kiosk in Vukovar and Borovo Naselje was blown up as well. Later on, it was rumoured that this had been done by former criminals, such as Darko Markobasic and the like. At the time, they were members of the Tomislav Merced Guards and that of Plisa Marin [phoen]. I remember that the first one to be blown up was the Sareka [phoen] kebab shop owned by Djordje Betic [phoen] near the market. I was especially shocked by that because that was the first terrorist attack. I knew the owner personally, and I frequently went to that place with my sons. Later on, the Borba kiosk at the market was blown up. The next one was the Brdo cafe near the log market." Now I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you still stand by your statement that you have never previously in any of your other statements mentioned Darko Markobasic? Or rather Davor Markobasic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wrote this down in prison, 14 years ago. I completely forget that I ever mentioned this. What actually happened here is that I heard this. I never personally witnessed anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we heard from the witness that she knows who Tomislav Mercep is. My question is as follows: In June of 1991, did Mercep, Tomislav limit the freedom of movement of the citizens of Vukovar and were there any permits issued and signed by him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he had some permits signed by him, or rather the staff of the All People's Defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard that due to the amount of work at the hospital, the witness, when asked by my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, answered something, and I will now put a question related to that. How is it that all of those faxed calls for help were not sent to Vinkovci or to the National Defence Staff through various help workers, drivers, and so on, or through the policemen securing the hospital? And why did she instead personally left the hospital daily in October and November in order to send a fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote these faxes personally. I believed them to be important. And I wanted to send them personally. Everybody had their tasks in the hospital. They were all busy. Every time one left the hospital, one exposed oneself to a great risk, and only if you were lucky and God protected you, you had a chance of staying alive. I did not want to expose anyone to the risk and send them out to send the fax. So that's why I did that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question is as follows: Did she have direct telephone line to the police, the Defence Staff in Vukovar, or that in Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a direct telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At a certain point in time, did the Serb patients stop coming to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "Serb patients"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Patients of Serbian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People of all ethnicities kept coming, Croats, Serbs, and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the answer is that the Serb patients didn't stop coming to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only patients who did not come to the hospital were those who were outside of the siege. Within the city of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje, patients of all ethnicities continuously came to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The next question I would like to show the witness Binazija Kolesar's statement. The OTP is, of course, in possession of this statement. 19th and 20th of June 1995, page 3, paragraph 1. The statement reads, "After the killing of the Croatian police officers in Borovo in 1991, Serb doctors and nurses started leaving their jobs at the hospital, saying that they were afraid of the return of the Ustashas who would then slit their throats. Many Serb patients likewise stopped going to the hospital. The overall number of patients decreased." Just another sentence: "From the Borovo Selo clash onwards, the hospital also treated wounded Croatian police officers but they were being guarded by armed police officers inside the hospital. It was then that the Serb civilian patients stopped going there because of the concern caused them by the presence of Croatian policemen at the hospital." My question for the witness is: What Binazija Kolesar is stating, is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, my information, patients from all ethnic backgrounds were coming to the hospital throughout. As for the Serb medical staff leaving, I would just like to say that some, and I emphasise "some" of the doctors and nurses did indeed stop coming to work. As for the other facts, you can't ask me that's true or not. According to the information I have, it is certainly not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We mentioned Mile Dedakovic, also known as Jastreb today. My question is, where was his headquarters in Vukovar? Does the witness know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the garden of a building that was being used as the All People's Defence secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was this a military facility?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, a barracks would be a military facility. This was just an every day, unmarked building that was being used as the All People's Defence secretariat. The headquarters of the staff itself was underground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In that same building?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The staff.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the garden of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Croatian police? Where did they have their own headquarters at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police building, which was near the Court building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, we've reached the time, I'm afraid. We just adjourn now and resume tomorrow at nine in the morning, if I could ask you to return then, doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
